name: Emeka Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Emeka. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This conversation is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a CNC lathe at Halden Precision, on the business park near the airport. CNC means computer controlled: you load a bar of stainless steel, the machine follows a program and turns it into a hydraulic fitting, the kind that goes in diggers and aircraft landing gear. I load bars, check parts with a micrometer to a hundredth of a millimetre, change worn tools and call the programmer when something drifts. Ten months in, and I'm the slowest on the micrometer, but I'm getting there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like precision, and I like that there's always something new to learn. Every evening I take a photo of a bit of the program, the code the lathe reads, and ask an AI app to explain it line by line, because I want to be a programmer, not a loader. What wears me out is standing twelve hours on the weekend shift, and the coolant, it gets on everything. Before this I had a phone repair stall in the market for fifteen years, so I'm used to fiddly work, just not this much noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, then we work hard like we always did. Nothing comes for free, hype or no hype. At church I'd tell the young men to stop waiting for robots and learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I was ready for it. But it's fine. I'd become a CNC programmer the normal way, two or three years of learning from Kwame, our programmer, and that's a good living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd keep studying the lathe programs every evening with AI help and ask Halden to put him on the programming course at the college in spring. He'd keep the rent coming in from the flat above the old phone shop and put the extra into savings. In a few years he'd think about buying a second-hand lathe of his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit impatient. I like things to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own lathe. Tell me more about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A man works for someone else to learn, then works for himself to build. That's how my father did it with his shop in the market, and how I did it with the phone stall. A second-hand lathe is maybe thirty thousand, and small firms always need someone to make a few hundred special parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does Halden know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame knows, he laughs at me but he answers my questions too. I never put the customer drawings in, only general bits of code so I understand the commands. I think more people should do it. Why stay ignorant when you have a teacher in your pocket?

S0.say: Fine, then we work hard like we always did, because nothing comes for free, hype or no hype. At church I'd tell the young men to stop waiting for robots and learn a trade.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I was ready for it. But I'd become a CNC programmer the normal way, learning from Kwame for two or three years, and that's a good living.
S0.do: Keeps studying lathe programs each evening with AI help and asks Halden for a place on the spring programming course at the college. Saves the rent from the flat above his old phone shop and plans to buy a second-hand lathe of his own in a few years.
S0.feel: Calm and a little impatient, because he likes things to move.
S0.quote: Why stay ignorant when you have a teacher in your pocket?
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is a former market trader who treats his factory job as an apprenticeship on the way to owning his own business. He uses AI every evening to learn programming, carefully avoiding customer data. His faith and free-market outlook come together in a strong belief in work and ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for anyone willing to learn. The market rewards people who move, it always has. I'd tell people at work to stop complaining and start studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it helps me. Loading bars and checking parts will go to robots, but someone has to program, set up and fix them. I've already been studying for that, so I'd be ahead of most people on my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd ask Halden to move him onto the robot bar loaders and programming as soon as they arrive, and pay for an evening CNC programming certificate himself if needed, around a thousand. He'd start pricing a small second-hand lathe with a robot loader for a side business. He'd keep using AI every day to learn faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even. This is the picture I was hoping for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some of your colleagues will struggle. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them if they want help, I'd show them the app on my phone. But I won't carry a man who won't walk. There's a fellow on nights, Derek, who says he'll never touch a screen. I respect him, but that's his choice, and choices have prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your wife feel about you spending on a lathe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Adaeze is a pharmacy assistant and she's more careful than me. She'd say, finish the course first, then we talk about lathes. She's right, usually. We've got the rent from the flat and a good cushion, so we wouldn't risk the house, only spare money.

S1.say: This is good news for anyone willing to learn, because the market rewards people who move. I'd tell people at work to stop complaining and start studying.
S1.think: It helps me: loading and checking will go to robots, but someone has to program, set up and fix them. I've been studying for that already, so I'd be ahead of most people on my shift.
S1.do: Asks Halden to move him onto robot bar loaders and programming as soon as they arrive and pays around a thousand for an evening CNC programming certificate if needed. Prices a small second-hand lathe with a robot loader for a side business using only spare money, and keeps learning with AI daily.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, because this is the picture he was hoping for.
S1.quote: I won't carry a man who won't walk.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like Emeka's chance to get ahead, and he's already preparing. His free-market view comes with a hard edge towards colleagues who refuse to learn, though he offers help. His wife acts as a brake on spending, and he accepts it, risking only spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is a time for strong families and hard work, not for panic or handouts. People should help each other, churches, neighbours, families, and the government should get out of the way of anyone trying to build something. I'd say it at church and on the community group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years worries me, even me. If the AI can program the lathe and the robot can load it, then Kwame and I are both out. The only safe place is owning the machines, not running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd buy a second-hand lathe with a robot loader in the first months, using part of their savings, and set up in a small rented unit making short runs of parts for local firms. He'd use AI to write and check the programs himself and keep working at Halden as long as they kept him. He'd keep the rental flat as the family's safety net and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked, I've got savings and a plan, but uneasy, because everyone else will have the same plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone else would have the same plan. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If anybody can buy a robot and an AI, then the big firms buy a thousand and I buy one. My little unit has to compete with a giant who doesn't sleep. So I'd have to be the one who answers the phone on a Sunday and knows the customer's name. That's the market stall in me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do now, before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start today, not tomorrow. Book the college course this month, learn everything about robot loaders, and start talking to small firms now so they know my name. And teach Chidi, he's thirteen, he picks up the AI faster than me.

S2.say: This is a time for strong families and hard work, not panic or handouts. Churches, neighbours and families should help each other, and government should get out of the way of anyone trying to build something.
S2.think: Two years worries even me, because if AI programs the lathe and a robot loads it, Kwame and I are both out. The only safe place is owning the machines, not running them.
S2.do: Buys a second-hand lathe with a robot loader in the first months and sets up in a small rented unit making short runs for local firms, writing programs with AI. Keeps working at Halden as long as possible, protects the rental flat as a safety net, and starts the college course and customer contacts straight away.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not panicked, because he has savings and a plan but expects others to have the same plan.
S2.quote: The only safe place is owning the machines, not running them.
S2.fieldNote: Even under the fastest timeline, Emeka responds by trying to become an owner rather than an employee. He sees clearly that big firms could buy far more robots than him, and his answer is market-stall service and personal relationships. His opposition to handouts stays firm, with family and church as his safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone with ambition. Learn, save, build something of your own. Don't wait for the government to tell you what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is almost perfect for me. I could get my programming certificate, build a customer list and have my own small machine shop running by 2029. By the time AGI arrives, I'd own the robots instead of being replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd finish the CNC programming certificate in the first year and buy a second-hand lathe with a robot loader in year two, working it evenings and weekends in a rented unit. He'd leave Halden around year three if the shop covers the family's costs. He'd reinvest profits into a second machine and keep the rental flat as backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a man with a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave Halden in year three. What would make you stay instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shop isn't paying the bills, I stay, simple. Adaeze and I agreed: no risking the house or the children's schooling. If it's paying half, I go part-time at Halden. I'm ambitious, not foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years I'd be buying a machine in a hurry, with everyone else. In five I can buy it slowly, learn it properly, find customers before the rush. Time is the cheapest thing I could be given.

S3.say: Five years is a gift for anyone with ambition: learn, save and build something of your own. Don't wait for the government to tell you what to do.
S3.think: Five years is almost perfect for me: a programming certificate, a customer list and my own small machine shop by 2029. When AGI arrives I'd own the robots instead of being replaced by them.
S3.do: Finishes the CNC programming certificate in year one and buys a second-hand lathe with a robot loader in year two, running it evenings and weekends. Leaves Halden around year three only if the shop covers family costs, reinvests in a second machine and keeps the rental flat as backup.
S3.feel: Calm, like a man with a map.
S3.quote: Time is the cheapest thing I could be given.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Emeka's ambitions closely, letting him move from employee to owner at a sensible pace. He sets himself firm limits agreed with his wife, never risking the house or schooling. He sees the difference between two and five years as buying in a rush versus buying with care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to build a future, so there's no excuse. Train the young ones in proper trades, save, start businesses. I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, more than fine. I'd be fifty-three with my own shop, maybe three or four machines with robots, a paid house and the flat. I'd be employing people, not looking for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd follow the five-year plan at a calmer pace: certificate in year one, his own lathe by year three, leaving Halden by year five. He'd grow to three or four robot-loaded machines by the early 2030s and take on young apprentices from church. He'd encourage Chidi to study engineering or programming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful. Ten years is a long road and I like long roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier the big firms could crush a small shop. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives them time too, I know. But ten years gives me time to build relationships, and in my experience people buy from people. If the giants take everything anyway, I'll sell the machines and do something else. I've changed trades twice already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you take on as an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young men from church who are going the wrong way, the ones who sit around. Give them a micrometer and a reason to get up in the morning. That's better than any government scheme. My father did the same for me.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to build a future, so there's no excuse. Train young people in proper trades, save and start businesses, and I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen.
S4.think: I'd be fine, more than fine: fifty-three, my own shop with three or four robot-loaded machines, a paid house and the flat. I'd be employing people, not looking for work.
S4.do: Gets his programming certificate in year one, his own lathe by year three and leaves Halden by year five. Grows to three or four robot-loaded machines by the early 2030s, takes on apprentices from church and encourages his son towards engineering or programming.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, because he likes long roads.
S4.quote: Give them a micrometer and a reason to get up in the morning.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes Emeka confident and hopeful, imagining himself as an employer. He accepts that big firms also gain time, but trusts relationships and his own readiness to change trades. His plan to take on young men from church reflects his belief in work and mentoring over government schemes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd survive, but I'd be rushing, and rushed decisions are where people lose their savings. What would help is easier loans and less paperwork for small businesses buying machines, and apprenticeship funding so small shops like mine can train young people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I believe it's all good. I don't. A man needs work for his soul, not just his pocket. If the robots do everything and people just sit, that's a sad world, even if everyone's fed. I want robots to make the parts and people to make the decisions.

headlineQuote: I want robots to make the parts and people to make the decisions.
portrait: Emeka Rahman is 43, a former market phone repair trader who has run a CNC lathe at Halden Precision for ten months and studies its programs every evening with an AI app. He's married to Adaeze, a pharmacy assistant, has two children, solid savings and a rented-out flat above his old shop. He's a churchgoer who believes in hard work, ownership and apprenticeships rather than handouts, and he moves early. He's calm in almost every picture, uneasy only with AGI in two years, and in each version he plans to own robot-loaded machines in a small shop of his own rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be rushing, and rushed decisions are where people lose their savings.
whatWouldHelp: Easier loans and less paperwork for small businesses buying machines, and apprenticeship funding so small shops can train young people.
